processing: A sheng recipe cake from Menghai Tea Factory, using mostly Menghai large-leaf maocha that is steamed and pressed.
harvest_season: A blended factory recipe, identified by production year rather than by a picking season.
appearance_dry: A pressed cake of dark olive large leaf, with aged examples turning browner.
appearance_liquor: Golden when young, and amber to red-brown in the aged cakes now on the market.
appearance_wet: Medium to large leaf in olive to brown tones, depending on age.
taste_profile: Described as smooth on the palate, from a fairly uniform grade of leaf; beyond that, specific tasting records are scarce.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for a factory sheng applies: a quick rinse and short early steeps, then longer as it fades.

vintage_note: Documented production runs are 2005 and 2006, so what circulates is aged cake sold by those years. Output was limited and the labels and inner tickets carry anti-counterfeit marks, which are worth checking. Storage history matters as much as the year.
description:
7742 is a Dayi recipe cake from Menghai Tea Factory, far less familiar than 7542 or 7532. It is a green, uncooked cake, and its appeal to collectors comes from limited production across only a couple of documented years.

The material is mostly Menghai large-leaf tea at a fairly narrow range of grades, so the profile is simpler than a wide blend. It is steamed and pressed like other factory cakes.

Drinkers mention smoothness above all. Since the documented batches are now about two decades old, expect the softer, darker cup of a mid-aged sheng rather than a sharp young one, with storage doing much to shape it. Brew it the way you would any factory sheng and adjust from there.

For a buyer, the checks are year, wrapper and the anti-counterfeit marks on label and inner ticket. Do not read the number like 7532: the first batch came decades after what the digits 77 would suggest under the usual reading of recipe codes.
history:
The tea is documented as a product of the mid-2000s, after Menghai Tea Factory became a private company. The first batch was made in 2005 and another followed in 2006, also known as 7742 Chenxiang Qingbing.

Little is documented about the recipe's design, or about later production.
